doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Radio: WBAI, The Scope of Jazz and Jazz from the Archives
summary: His radio work from WBAI in the sixties to WBGO's 'Jazz from the Archives', and his roughly 700 liner notes.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: It helped inform their choices of what to play, yeah, sure. It made them sound more informed.

And actually, one of the reasons why I did that, although I didn’t start initially, was that I’ve done quite a lot of radio over time. I started out at WBAI in New York. And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” And Martin had to bow out and he turned it over to me. And so, that was back in the sixties. Nat Hentoff was also in it. Gunther was the first one and then he moved to Boston. Anyway, it was © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

like a series, one hour jazz, a Sunday night broadcast. But then once I got with the Institute we started, when WBGO was the new jazz radio station in Newark back thirty- some years ago, they came to us at the Institute and asked us to do a weekly program, and we decided to call it “Jazz from the Archives.” And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program. We started out, the station didn’t have very much. They had no record library. We of course had a huge library. So early days we were three hours a week and then later it was back to two and now for the last 15 years or so it’s been a one hour show. But anyway, I’ve done a lot of radio. Nat’s very useful when you play records on the air, to be able to look at a liner note and see what it says about the tune and so on. Anyway the liner notes, when I was still at Rutgers the very nice library director Lynn Mullins who was a great fan of the Institute’s, and she wanted a bibliography of my liner notes. And at that time my younger son Josh was still in school, actually he was — well he got his B.A. from the University of Chicago but then he went to law school first to Brooklyn College and then Columbia. But he had some time in the summer so he put this thing together. But I couldn’t even remember all the notes that I did, and it adds up to hundreds and hundreds, something like 700.
